Overview

Goal: Understand how tuition, financial burden, and institutional characteristics relate to post-graduation earnings.
Data: U.S. Department of Education College Scorecard
Methods:

Exploratory data analysis
Linear & Ridge regression
Logistic regression & Random Forest

Key focus: Which institutional features most strongly predict higher earnings 10 years after enrollment?

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings
text:
Research Questions

RQ1. How do tuition and financial burden relate to median earnings 10 years after enrollment?
RQ2. How do institutional characteristics (region, locale, control, size) and student composition (Pell share) relate to earnings and completion?
RQ3. Can institutional features reliably classify colleges as high-earning vs. low-earning?
RQ4. Which features are most important for prediction across linear and machine-learning models?

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings
text:
Data & Preprocessing

Source: U.S. College Scorecard (institution-level data).
Scope:

Filtered to institutions that primarily award bachelor’s degrees.
Focused on recent cohorts with available 10-year earnings.

Key variable groups:

Cost: in-state & out-of-state tuition, median debt.
Institutional: enrollment (UGDS), control, region, locale.
Outcomes: retention, 4-year completion, 10-year median earnings.

Missing data:

Dropped columns with severe missingness (e.g., detailed demographics).
Dropped rows with missing core cost/outcome variables rather than imputing.

text:
Exploratory Data Analysis

Cost:

In-state and out-of-state tuition are right-skewed.
Most schools between ≈ $10K–$40K; a small number of very expensive institutions.

Size (UGDS):

Strong right skew; most enroll 1K–6K students.
A few very large institutions (e.g., large online providers).

Outcomes:

Retention and completion rates are bounded [0,1] and cluster toward higher values.
Identified and removed institutions with impossible patterns (e.g., 0% completion at all time horizons, 0% retention with missing context).

Earnings:

10-year earnings percentiles are skewed; median earnings used as a stable target.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings
text:
Correlation Patterns

Tuition has only weak to moderate correlation with earnings.
Retention and completion rates show moderate positive correlations with earnings.
Pell Grant share (PCTPELL) shows negative correlations with both earnings and completion:

Institutions serving more low-income students tend to have lower median earnings.

Takeaway: Institutional performance and student composition are more strongly related to outcomes than tuition alone.

Linear Regression Results

Adjusted R² ≈ 0.57 — institutional features explain over half of the variation in 10-year earnings.

Largest negative coefficients: Pell Grant share (PCTPELL), median student debt, and several lower-earning regional indicators.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings
text:
Key Findings

Higher tuition is associated with higher earnings, but:

Effects are modest and intertwined with other institutional features.

Retention and completion rates are strong, consistent predictors of long-term earnings.
Institutions with higher Pell Grant shares tend to have lower earnings, reflecting underlying socioeconomic differences.
Model performance:

Linear and Ridge regression explain ~50–57% of earnings variation.
Classification models distinguish high- vs low-earning institutions with F1 ≈ 0.77–0.82.

Student outcomes and composition matter at least as much as sticker price.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings
text:
Limitations & Future Work

Data limitations:

Institution-level aggregates; no student-level or major-level detail.
Missing data and reporting differences across institutions.

No causal claims:

Observational, cross-sectional analysis; cannot separate institution effect from selection bias.

Future directions:

Incorporate program and major details.
Examine changes over time (longitudinal trends).

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings
text:
Takeaways

Tuition alone is an incomplete indicator of value.
Academic success metrics (retention & completion) and student demographics are central to explaining earnings.
Machine-learning models provide modest gains in accuracy over linear models but highlight similar core drivers.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Increasing concern about the cost and value of higher education has increased interest in understanding how institutional characteristics, and cost relate to student outcomes, particularly earning after graduation. This project uses institution-level data from the U.S. Department of Education’s College Scorecard to investigate how tuition, institutional features, and student enrollment are associated with median earnings 10 years after enrollment. Additionally, it aims to assess the extent to which these variables can predict higher-earning graduates.
The dataset is restricted to institutions that primarily award bachelor’s degrees, and report complete information on 10-year earnings and core cost and outcome variables. After filtering and cleaning, the resulting sample retains a diverse set of institutions across regions, control types, and locale categories. To model earnings as a continuous outcome, the project applies both ordinary least squares (OLS) and Ridge regression. The OLS model explains a substantial portion of the variation in 10-year earnings, with retention, completion, and in-state tuition emerging as strong positive predictors, and median debt and Pell share showing negative associations. Ridge regression provides comparable predictive accuracy while better handling multicollinearity among financial variables.
A classification task reframes the problem by labeling institutions as high-earning or low-earning relative to the sample median. Feature selection using statistical tests, random forest importance, and permutation importance identifies a consistent set of influential predictors, including enrollment size, retention, completion, tuition, and Pell share. Logistic regression and random forest models are then trained on the selected feature set. Both models achieve strong performance, with F1 scores around 0.77–0.82. Calibration curves show that each model produces reasonably reliable probability estimates, with logistic regression slightly smoother and more aligned with observed frequencies.
Overall, the results suggest that while tuition contributes to differences in earnings, institutional performance indicators and student composition play a larger role. Earnings outcomes reflect a combination of institutional characteristics and the demographic and academic profile of the students they serve, highlighting the complexity of evaluating value in higher education.

Introduction
The rising cost of higher education in the United States has intensified concerns about whether attending college is worth it for students. Families increasingly weigh tuition, financial aid, and borrowing against expected earnings after graduation, yet the relationships between these factors and long-term outcomes are complex and difficult to observe directly. This project uses the U.S. Department of Education’s College Scorecard dataset to investigate how institutional cost, student composition, and academic performance are associated with post-graduation earnings.
The analysis focuses on bachelor’s-degree-granting institutions and examines three main domains: cost of attendance (tuition and student debt), institutional characteristics (enrollment, sector, region, and locale), and student outcomes (retention, completion, and earnings). Two complementary modeling strategies are used. First, linear and penalized regression models estimate how these factors relate to median earnings ten years after enrollment. Second, logistic regression and random forest classifiers predict whether an institution falls above or below the sample median earnings level and identify which features are most important for classification. The goal is not to make causal claims, but to characterize patterns in the data and highlight which institutional features are most strongly associated with economic outcomes for graduates.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Data Preprocessing
The first preprocessing step involved separating the College Scorecard dataset into smaller CSV files due to GitHub’s file size restrictions. Dividing the dataset enabled successful upload and version control. Once stored in the repository, the individual files were reassembled to create a complete dataset that was saved for future use.
A subset of variables was then selected to represent three important factors: cost metrics, institutional characteristics, and student outcome measures. These categories were chosen to capture factors related to university prestige, which will impact cost, overall financial burden of attendance, and student success.
The dataset was further restricted by selecting institutions that primarily award bachelor’s degrees. This decision reflects structural differences in educational pathways across types of schools. For example, retention and completion rates could be defined inconsistently for two-year or certificate programs, where many students enroll without the intention of completing a degree. Additionally, undergraduate degrees were prioritized because graduate school outcomes will likely be very different and impacted highly by field of study. Limiting the dataset to primarily bachelor’s–degree-granting institutions ensures that outcome measures are comparable.
Next, there was a significant amount of missing values in the dataset. Columns such as demographic columns and certain expense columns were removed from the dataset due to a large amount of missing values and inability to confidently impute missing values. No values were imputed to prioritize data fidelity, since missing values could have resulted from institutional reporting practices or idiosyncrasies.
Prior to examining individual variables, the distribution of institutions from a geological and control (private vs. public) perspective were examined to ensure that filtering steps did not inadvertently remove entire regions. Histograms comparing the original and cleaned datasets show that U.S. regions and control groups remain represented similarly.

Exploratory Data analysis
After preprocessing and initial variable selection, an exploratory data analysis was conducted to understand the distribution of key variables, identify structural patterns in the dataset, and evaluate suitability of each variable. The EDA focuses on the three major domains described previously: cost of attendance, institutional characteristics, and student outcomes.
A series of histograms was generated for each numerical variable retained in the dataset.

Figure 4. Histograms of all retained numerical variables.
When looking at the cost metrics, in-state and out-of-state tuition both skewed to the right, with most institutions clustered between $10,000 and $40,000. There were some schools that had much higher tuition rates, which likely suggest highly selective and prodigious universities.
Considering the institutional characteristics, enrollment size shows a severe right skew, with most institutions enrolling between 1,000 and 6,000 undergraduates. However there is a long tail of universities with the maximum enrollment of 156,755. This outlier is Southern New Hampshire University. This institution has both in-person and online campuses that contributes to the large number of students. Since this represents a meaningful difference, no outlier removal was performed, though log-transformations may be used for visualization. Next, the student-to-faculty ratio is highly skewed, driven by a small number of likely specialized institutions with unusually high ratios. This can vary greatly depending on how schools report these numbers, so this column was removed before further analysis was conducted. Finally, the completion and retention rates are bounded between 0 and 1, with many institutions clustered toward the high end of the distribution. There are several schools with 0% completion rate within 4 years, but with completion rates existing for 6 and 8 years. Schools which had 0% completion for 4, 6, and 8 years were removed from the data since they may indicate errors or initially unreported data. Similarly, there were three schools with 0% retention rates. One of these schools is closed, so it does not have retention data, and the other two seem to be missing the data. Here, as well, the schools with 0% retention were removed from the dataset.
For the outcome metrics, debt measures appear approximately normally distributed with not extreme outliers. Earning percentiles show a strong right skew, reflecting the wide variation in early-career earnings across institutions. The median earnings follow a more moderate skew and can be used as a more stable proxy for early-career earnings.
A correlation matrix was created to begin to understand the relationships present in the dataset.

The correlation analysis demonstrates that tuition levels have relatively weak associations with student outcomes, while institutional performance metrics such as retention and completion rates show moderate positive relationships with earnings. Conversely, the share of Pell recipients is negatively associated with both earnings and completion measures, highlighting the influence of student socioeconomic background. These patterns suggest that institutional characteristics and student demographics have stronger relationships with outcomes than the price of attendance.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Models

Linear Regression
For the regression analysis, the target feature is the median earnings after 10 years. This was selected since it captures a large span of time, and will be less influenced by institutional differences than completion and retention. This allows for a more clear relationship between financial features, while still controlling for differences in institution type and locale. Skewed variables were log transformed, and all the features not already on a 0 to 1 scale were scaled.
Diagnostic plots indicate that the linear model is reasonably well-specified. Residuals were centered around zero with no systematic patterns, suggesting that the linearity assumption holds. Some heteroscedasticity is present in mid-range predicted values, and a long right-tail appears in the residual distribution and Q–Q plot, driven by a small number of high-earning institutions. Despite these limitations, predicted values align closely with observed values, indicating that the model captures substantial variation in earnings after graduation.
Variance inflation factors (VIFs) were examined to assess multicollinearity. Most predictors had VIF values below 5, indicating low multicollinearity. Tuition variables showed higher VIFs due to strong correlation between in-state and out-of-state tuition. To address this, out-of-state tuition was removed, and the model retained only in-state tuition as the primary cost predictor.
Although Pell Grant share and the private nonprofit indicator had VIFs slightly above 10, these were retained because they represent essential institutional characteristics related to socioeconomic composition and governance. Their inclusion was theoretically justified despite moderate multicollinearity.
After removing the highly collinear variable out-of-state tuition, the linear regression model remained stable with an adjusted R² of 0.566, indicating that the selected institutional characteristics explain approximately 57% of the variation in median earnings ten years after enrollment. The revised model substantially reduced multicollinearity and produced more interpretable coefficients.
The OLS coefficient plot highlights several clear patterns in how institutional features relate to median earnings 10 years after enrollment. The strongest positive predictors are in-state tuition, first-year retention (RET_FT4), four-year completion rates (C100_4), and enrollment size (UGDS). These variables reflect institutional resources and student success—factors that consistently align with higher post-graduation earnings.
On the negative side, PCTPELL (share of Pell Grant recipients) is the most influential predictor, indicating that institutions serving more low-income students tend to report lower median earnings, a pattern likely driven by socioeconomic factors rather than institutional quality alone. Several regional indicators (e.g., Southeast, Rocky Mountains, Outlying Areas) and rural locale categories also show negative associations, suggesting geographic labor-market effects.
Overall, the coefficient patterns reinforce that student success metrics and institutional characteristics—rather than cost alone—play the largest role in explaining variation in long-term earnings across colleges.

Feature Selection for Classification
To simplify the model and focus on the most informative predictors, two feature selection methods were applied. First, SelectKBest identified the top 15 variables most strongly associated with the high- vs. low-earnings outcome. Second, a Random Forest classifier was used to rank features by importance, capturing nonlinear effects and interactions. The final feature set was created by taking the union of the top features from both methods, ensuring that only the most relevant predictors were retained for classification.

text:
Evalutation
Overall, the regression and classification results tell a consistent story. The ordinary least squares and Ridge regression models explain roughly half of the variation in median earnings ten years after enrollment, with in-state tuition, retention, completion, and Pell share emerging as key predictors. However, diagnostic plots show curvature, heteroscedasticity, and heavy-tailed residuals, indicating that linear models do not fully capture the structure of the data and should be interpreted primarily as describing average trends rather than providing precise predictions for individual institutions.
The classification models perform somewhat better from a predictive standpoint. Logistic regression achieves an accuracy of about 0.77 with a cross-validated F1 of approximately 0.80, showing that a simple linear decision boundary can distinguish high- and low-earning institutions with reasonable accuracy. The random forest classifier improves performance slightly (accuracy ≈ 0.78, F1 ≈ 0.82) by capturing nonlinear relationships and interactions among predictors. However, calibration curves show that logistic regression produces far better-calibrated probability estimates, while the random forest tends to be overconfident. Permutation importance results align with earlier findings, emphasizing student body size, retention, completion, tuition, and Pell share as the most influential features. The modest accuracy gain from random forest suggests that although nonlinear effects exist, much of the signal is already captured by the linear model.
Several limitations should be noted. The analysis is based on cross-sectional, institution-level aggregates and cannot separate institutional effects from differences in student populations, academic programs, or local impacts. Important factors such as major, selectivity, and student academic preparation are not modeled explicitly. In addition, missing data and reporting variation in the College Scorecard may introduce noise or bias. Finally, all models estimate associations rather than causal effects. Higher tuition or higher retention may correlate with earnings for reasons unrelated to the policies of a particular institution.

title: Predicting Post-Graduation Earnings Using Tuition, Institutional Metrics, and Student Demographics
text:
Conclusion
This project examined how tuition, financial burden, institutional characteristics, and student success metrics relate to post-graduation earnings using the College Scorecard dataset. Across both regression and classification approaches, tuition and student debt measures were associated with earnings, but institutional performance and student composition were as important. Institutions with higher retention and completion rates tended to have higher median earnings, while those serving larger shares of Pell Grant recipients tended to have lower earnings, consistent with underlying socioeconomic differences. Regional indicators also played a role, reflecting geographic wage disparities.
The modeling results suggest that the cost of an institution is an imperfect proxy for long-term outcomes. Higher-tuition institutions often have stronger earnings, but this relationship is intertwined with selectivity, student demographics, and academic success. Classification models show that a combination of enrollment size, retention, completion, tuition, and Pell share provides the strongest predictive power, while fine-grained locale categories and control type contribute relatively little once other factors are accounted for.
Future work could extend this analysis by incorporating program-level data (e.g., major fields), longitudinal trends over multiple cohorts, or student-level information where available. Methods such as causal inference or matching designs could help disentangle institutional impact from student selection. Nevertheless, the findings here provide a useful descriptive map of how cost, institutional characteristics, and student outcomes align with graduates’ early-career earnings across U.S. colleges and universities.
